name: Sample papers
description: 35 hand-written questions over the five bundled sample papers: factual questions, paraphrases that share few words with the paper, keyword questions about exact numbers or names, questions that need two papers, and questions the papers cannot answer.

papers.proxavg: ProxAvg: Proximal Local Objectives for Federated Optimization on Heterogeneous Devices
papers.driftguard: DriftGuard: Correcting Client Drift in Federated Learning with Control Variates
papers.fuserank: FuseRank: Combining Lexical and Dense Retrieval for Grounded Question Answering
papers.layeralign: LayerAlign: Compact Student Models through Layer-Aligned Knowledge Distillation
papers.solvgat: SolvGAT: Graph Attention Networks for Predicting Aqueous Solubility of Small Molecules

questions.question: What does ProxAvg add to each device's local objective?

evidence.text: Instead of minimising its local loss alone, device k minimises the local loss plus a penalty equal to mu divided by two times the squared distance between its weights and the global weights received at the start of the round.

questions.reference_answer: A proximal penalty: mu/2 times the squared distance between the device's weights and the global weights from the start of the round, which keeps local models close to the global model.

questions.question: How does the proximal method deal with phones that cannot finish their assigned training in time?

evidence.text: ProxAvg also accepts partial work, letting slow devices return fewer local steps instead of being dropped.
the server accepts whatever a device returns by the deadline rather than discarding stragglers.

questions.reference_answer: It accepts partial work: slow devices return whatever local progress they made by the deadline instead of being dropped.

questions.question: Which value of mu worked best on Shakespeare?

evidence.text: mu equal to 0.01 worked best on Shakespeare and mu equal to 1 on MNIST.

questions.question: Which datasets are used to evaluate ProxAvg?

evidence.text: We evaluate on four federated benchmarks. MNIST and FEMNIST are image classification tasks

questions.reference_answer: MNIST, FEMNIST, Shakespeare and Sent140.

questions.question: What assumption does the ProxAvg convergence analysis rely on?

evidence.text: We analyse ProxAvg under a bounded dissimilarity assumption, which limits how different the gradients of local objectives can be from the global gradient.
Our convergence analysis relies on the bounded dissimilarity assumption, which may not hold for adversarial or extremely skewed federations.

questions.reference_answer: Bounded dissimilarity: the local gradients cannot differ too much from the global gradient. The authors note it may not hold for adversarial or extremely skewed federations.

questions.question: How much better is the proximal approach than plain averaging when the data across devices is very uneven?

evidence.text: On the most heterogeneous partitions ProxAvg improves absolute test accuracy by 18 percentage points on average over plain averaging.

questions.reference_answer: About 18 percentage points of absolute test accuracy on average on the most heterogeneous partitions.

questions.question: What is client drift?

evidence.text: on heterogeneous data each client moves toward the minimiser of its own loss. We call this effect client drift.

questions.reference_answer: On heterogeneous data, each client's local steps move it toward the minimiser of its own loss instead of the global one.

questions.question: How many communication rounds does DriftGuard need to reach 0.5 test accuracy on EMNIST?

evidence.text: On EMNIST, DriftGuard reaches 0.5 test accuracy in 31 rounds, compared with 148 rounds for federated averaging and 92 rounds for the proximal baseline.

questions.reference_answer: 31 rounds, compared with 148 for federated averaging and 92 for the proximal baseline.

questions.question: What extra cost does the control-variate method impose on the network?

evidence.text: The price is that each round transmits a correction vector in addition to the model, which doubles the upload size.
DriftGuard doubles the upload per round because each client sends its control variate update together with the model update.

questions.reference_answer: It doubles the upload per round, because each client sends its control variate update along with the model update.

questions.question: How does DriftGuard correct each local gradient step?

evidence.text: During local training, client i corrects every stochastic gradient by subtracting c_i and adding c, so that its update follows the global direction rather than its local one.

questions.reference_answer: Each stochastic gradient is corrected by subtracting the client control variate c_i and adding the server control variate c, so the update follows the global direction.

questions.question: What learning rate, number of local epochs and batch size do DriftGuard clients use?

evidence.text: Clients use a learning rate of 0.05 and five local epochs with a batch size of 50.

questions.reference_answer: A learning rate of 0.05, five local epochs and a batch size of 50.

questions.question: Why is the method a poor fit for devices that take part in training only once?

evidence.text: Clients must also store their control variate between rounds, which is a problem for clients that participate only once or rarely, since their stored variate becomes stale.

questions.reference_answer: Clients have to keep their control variate between rounds, and for clients that participate once or rarely the stored variate becomes stale.

questions.question: How does FuseRank combine the dense and BM25 rankings?

evidence.text: it uses reciprocal rank fusion, which gives each passage the sum of one divided by k plus its rank in each list, with k equal to 60.

questions.reference_answer: With reciprocal rank fusion: each passage scores the sum of 1/(k + rank) over both lists, with k = 60, instead of combining raw scores.

questions.question: What recall at 10 does BM25 reach on TechDocQA?

evidence.text: Dense retrieval reaches a recall at 10 of 0.71 and BM25 reaches 0.64, but on questions with exact identifiers BM25 is better by 19 points.

questions.reference_answer: 0.64, although BM25 is 19 points better than dense retrieval on questions with exact identifiers.

questions.question: What weakness of neural embeddings motivates adding keyword search?

evidence.text: Embedding models map questions and passages into a shared vector space, which captures meaning but blurs exact strings such as error codes, version numbers and product names.

questions.reference_answer: Embeddings capture meaning but blur exact strings such as error codes, version numbers and product names.

questions.question: How much latency does the cross-encoder add in FuseRank?

evidence.text: The cross-encoder adds about 120 milliseconds of latency per question on a CPU, which may be too slow for interactive use on large candidate sets.

questions.reference_answer: About 120 milliseconds per question on a CPU.

questions.question: How many passages does FuseRank pass to the generator after reranking?

evidence.text: The top 20 fused candidates are then scored by a cross-encoder that reads the question and each passage together, and the best eight passages are passed to the generator.

questions.reference_answer: Eight, chosen by the cross-encoder from the top 20 fused candidates.

questions.question: By how much does the full system reduce answers that make claims the sources do not back up?

evidence.text: Unsupported claims in generated answers fall from 14 percent with dense retrieval to 6 percent with FuseRank.

questions.reference_answer: Unsupported claims fall from 14 percent with dense retrieval to 6 percent with FuseRank.

questions.question: How does LayerAlign decide which teacher layer each student layer should imitate?

evidence.text: LayerAlign first measures how similar each teacher layer is to each student layer at initialisation using centred kernel alignment on a small batch of unlabelled text.
It then solves a monotone assignment problem so that lower student layers map to lower teacher layers and the total similarity is maximised.

questions.reference_answer: It measures layer similarity with centred kernel alignment at initialisation, then solves a monotone assignment that maps lower student layers to lower teacher layers while maximising total similarity.

questions.question: What temperature is used for the softened outputs in LayerAlign?

evidence.text: the cross-entropy between softened teacher and student outputs with a temperature of 4

questions.reference_answer: A temperature of 4.

questions.question: How much faster is the six-layer compressed model, and how much of the original quality does it keep?

evidence.text: The six-layer student keeps 97 percent of the average GLUE score of the teacher and is 2.1 times faster

questions.reference_answer: It is 2.1 times faster and keeps 97 percent of the teacher's average GLUE score.

questions.question: Why can this technique not compress models that are only offered through a hosted service?

evidence.text: LayerAlign requires access to the internal states of the teacher, so it cannot distil from models that are only available through an API.

questions.reference_answer: It needs the teacher's internal states, which models available only through an API do not expose.

questions.question: Which loss matters most in the LayerAlign ablation?

evidence.text: Removing the attention loss costs one point on average, and removing the hidden-state loss costs three.

questions.reference_answer: The hidden-state loss: removing it costs three points, against one point for the attention loss.

questions.question: What error does SolvGAT achieve on the ESOL test split?

evidence.text: SolvGAT reaches a root mean squared error of 0.52 log units on the scaffold test split

questions.reference_answer: A root mean squared error of 0.52 log units on the scaffold test split.

questions.question: Which chemical groups does the model pay most attention to?

evidence.text: Visualising attention shows that hydroxyl, amine and carboxyl groups receive the highest weights, consistent with their known effect on solubility.

questions.reference_answer: Hydroxyl, amine and carboxyl groups.

questions.question: How many molecules are in the ESOL dataset?

evidence.text: We use the ESOL dataset of 1,128 molecules with measured aqueous solubility

questions.reference_answer: 1,128 molecules.

questions.question: What features represent each atom in SolvGAT?

evidence.text: SolvGAT represents each atom by its element, degree, formal charge, hybridisation and aromaticity

questions.reference_answer: Its element, degree, formal charge, hybridisation and aromaticity.

questions.question: What physical factors does the solubility model leave out?

evidence.text: SolvGAT ignores three-dimensional conformation and temperature, both of which affect solubility.

questions.reference_answer: Three-dimensional conformation and temperature.

questions.question: How do ProxAvg and DriftGuard differ in how they handle heterogeneous client data?

evidence.text: Instead of minimising its local loss alone, device k minimises the local loss plus a penalty equal to mu divided by two times the squared distance between its weights and the global weights received at the start of the round.
During local training, client i corrects every stochastic gradient by subtracting c_i and adding c, so that its update follows the global direction rather than its local one.

questions.reference_answer: ProxAvg adds a proximal penalty that keeps local weights near the global model, while DriftGuard corrects every local gradient with control variates so updates follow the global direction.

questions.question: Which datasets do the two federated learning papers evaluate on?

evidence.text: We evaluate on four federated benchmarks. MNIST and FEMNIST are image classification tasks
We evaluate DriftGuard on the extended MNIST dataset EMNIST with 400 simulated clients

questions.reference_answer: ProxAvg uses MNIST, FEMNIST, Shakespeare and Sent140; DriftGuard uses EMNIST and CIFAR-10.

questions.question: What assumptions limit the convergence theory of the two federated learning methods?

evidence.text: Our convergence analysis relies on the bounded dissimilarity assumption, which may not hold for adversarial or extremely skewed federations.
Our theory assumes full gradients for the variance analysis and strongly convex losses for the main rate.

questions.reference_answer: ProxAvg assumes bounded dissimilarity between local and global gradients; DriftGuard assumes full gradients for its variance analysis and strongly convex losses for its main rate.
